steps.user_message: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Austin TX. W-2 from Coastal Manufacturing: $96,500. Additional income: $18,400 (photography, 5 clients), $2,100 from Capital One 360, $670 from Schwab. Home office: 120 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,750/month for 720 sq ft. Deductions: $3,200 student loan interest (Great Lakes, 2019–2021); $950 to Salvation Army have the receipt; $540 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Quick overview first — I can give a more exact recommendation if you confirm two things (see questions below). Below is a clear, practical summary based on the facts you gave and some conservative assumptions.

Clarifying questions
- When you say “file my 2024 taxes,” do you mean the return for tax year 2024 (the return you’d file in 2025) or the return you will file in calendar year 2024 (i.e., tax year 2023)? The rules below assume you mean tax year 2024.
- Is the $3,200 student‑loan interest the amount paid in the tax year you’re filing? (Only interest paid in the tax year is deductible and is reported on the 1098‑E.)
- Are the $540 “unreimbursed expenses” expenses related to your photography business (self‑employment)? Or are they unreimbursed employee expenses from a W‑2 job? (Only self‑employment expenses are deductible on Schedule C now; unreimbursed employee expenses are not deductible for most taxpayers.)

What you can and can’t deduct (summary)
- Photography income ($18,400): Report on Schedule C (self‑employment). You can deduct ordinary and necessary business expenses related to the photography work (supplies, business mileage, advertising, client costs, equipment depreciation, home‑office portion of rent if qualifying, etc.).
- Home office: You have a dedicated 120 sq ft space in a 720 sq ft rental. If this space is used regularly and exclusively for the business and the home office is your principal place of business (or used to meet clients, store inventory, etc.), you may take a home‑office deduction.
  - Two methods:
    - Simplified: $5 per sq ft up to 300 sq ft → 120 sq ft × $5 = $600.
    - Regular (actual) method: allocate the business percentage of home expenses. Your business percentage = 120/720 = 1/6 ≈ 16.6667%. Annual rent = $1,750 × 12 = $21,000. Rent portion attributable to the office = $21,000 × 1/6 = $3,500. (If you have utilities, renter’s insurance, internet, etc., their business portion could also be included under the regular method, increasing the deduction.) Because 3,500 > 600, the actual method will likely give you a larger deduction unless you have no other home expenses to allocate.
  - If you use the actual method, you will normally use Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) along with Schedule C. With the simplified method, you report the simplified deduction on Schedule C.
- Interest income ($2,100 + $670 = $2,770): Taxable interest. Because total interest > $1,500, you’ll likely need Schedule B (Form 1040, Schedule B) and include the 1099‑INTs you receive.
- Student loan interest ($3,200): The student loan interest deduction is an above‑the‑line deduction (adjustment to income), up to $2,500 maximum (subject to MAGI phaseouts). Important:
  - Only interest paid in the tax year can be deducted and only to the extent shown on Form 1098‑E from your loan servicer.
  - The deduction phases out based on your modified adjusted gross income (MAGI). If your MAGI is above the phaseout threshold for the year, the deduction will be reduced or eliminated. (I can check approximate eligibility once we calculate your MAGI.)
- Charitable donations ($950): Charitable contributions are itemized deductions. If you take the standard deduction, you cannot also claim these (except limited special rules in some years). The deduction requires a receipt for cash donations (which you have).
- Unreimbursed employee expenses ($540): If these are unreimbursed employee expenses from a W‑2 job, they are not deductible for tax years 2018–2025 under current law (TCJA). If they are business expenses for the photography self‑employment, they are deductible on Schedule C.

Self‑employment tax and related deduction
- You will owe self‑employment (SE) tax on net self‑employment earnings (Schedule SE). SE tax is ~15.3% on net earnings (net business profit × 92.35% × 15.3%). You can deduct one‑half of SE tax as an above‑the‑line deduction on Form 1040, which reduces your AGI.

Estimate (illustrative) — tells you whether itemize or standard is likely better
(These are estimates to illustrate which deduction route is likely best. I’ll refine if you confirm the clarifying items above.)

1) Income (approximate)
- W‑2 wages: $96,500
- Net self‑employment income (photography): $18,400 gross − business expenses.
  - If you use actual home office and include rent portion $3,500 and the $540 business expenses: business expenses ≈ $4,040 → net SE income ≈ $14,360.
- Interest income: $2,770
- Estimated AGI before SE tax deduction and student loan interest: 96,500 + 14,360 + 2,770 = $113,630

2) Above‑the‑line deductions
- Half of SE tax (estimate): Net SE profit 14,360 × 0.9235 = 13,265 → SE tax ≈ 13,265 × 15.3% ≈ $2,030 → half ≈ $1,015
- Student loan interest: up to $2,500 (limit) and subject to MAGI phaseout — you said $3,200 but only up to $2,500 is allowed and only if your MAGI is below the phaseout range.
- Adjusted gross income (roughly): 113,630 − 1,015 − (up to 2,500) ≈ 110,115 (if full $2,500 allowed).

3) Itemized deductions available from what you listed:
- Charitable: $950
- State income tax: $0 (Texas)
- Mortgage interest, property tax, large medical: none listed
=> Total itemized ≈ $950 (so standard deduction will almost certainly be larger).

Conclusion on standard vs itemize
- With only $950 of itemized deductions shown, the standard deduction will be larger. So you should take the standard deduction unless you have significant additional itemizable deductions (mortgage interest, sizable property taxes, large medical expenses, other charitable gifts, or large unreimbursed business expenses that aren’t otherwise deducted on Schedule C).
- The student loan interest deduction is not an itemized deduction — it’s an above‑the‑line adjustment and does not affect the choice of taking the standard deduction.

Forms you’ll likely need
- Form 1040 (U.S. Individual Income Tax Return)
- Schedule 1 (additional income and adjustments) — student loan interest deduction shows here (depending on current form layout; the software will place it correctly)
- Schedule B — if taxable interest is more than $1,500 or you have certain foreign accounts
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — report photography income and business expenses
- Schedule SE — calculate self‑employment tax
- Form 8829 — if you use the regular (actual) home office method
- Form 1098‑E — student loan interest statement (to support student loan interest deduction)
- Form(s) 1099‑INT — for interest income
- Any 1099‑NEC or 1099‑K you received for photography work (report on Schedule C)

Other important items and recommendations
- Estimated tax payments: Because you have SE income and SE tax liability, you may need to make quarterly estimated tax payments (Form 1040‑ES) or increase withholding on your W‑2 to avoid underpayment penalties.
- Recordkeeping: Keep receipts for business expenses, charitable donation receipts, 1099s, bank statements, and a simple floor plan/photos showing the exclusive use of the home office in case of IRS questions.
- Student loan interest phaseout: The student loan interest deduction phases out based on MAGI. Given your income level, the deduction might be reduced or eliminated — we should compute MAGI precisely (I can do that if you confirm the items I asked about).
- If you have equipment purchases, consider Section 179 or bonus depreciation for business assets; otherwise, depreciate them properly on Schedule C.
- If some of the $18,400 was paid via platforms that issue 1099‑K instead of 1099‑NEC, still report all income on Schedule C.

How I can help next
- I can run an exact estimate of taxable income and tax owed if you confirm:
  1) Whether the $3,200 in student loan interest was paid in the tax year you’re filing and whether you have Form 1098‑E.
  2) Whether the $540 unreimbursed expenses are business expenses for photography (or employee expenses).
  3) Any other deductible items (mortgage interest, property taxes, larger donations, medical expenses).
  4) Any utilities, insurance, internet costs for the home (to refine home‑office actual method).
- If you want, I can produce a step‑by‑step worksheet (with numbers) showing AGI, taxable income, SE tax, and whether you should take standard vs itemized.

If you’d like a quick estimate now, reply with answers to the 4 clarifying items above and I’ll calculate an estimated AGI, itemized vs standard comparison, and estimated federal tax + self‑employment tax.
